lead: A cantilever retaining wall holds back soil. The stem is vertical and fixed into a base slab. The heel of the slab carries soil; the toe sticks out in front. Soil pushes the stem, which bends as a cantilever. The whole wall must not tip, slide or sink. These walls appear at basements, road embankments, ramps and plot boundaries. The wall is checked for stability first, then stem, heel and toe are designed.
prereq: You need cantilever bending and shear from Unit 2, footing sizing by bearing pressure from 5.5, and bar detailing from Unit 3.

blocks.text: The stem is the vertical wall. The base slab lies under it. The slab behind the stem is the heel; the part in front is the toe. Soil on the heel stabilizes the wall. The stem acts as a vertical cantilever fixed to the base; heel and toe act as horizontal cantilevers fixed to the stem.
For dry, level, cohesionless backfill, pressure grows linearly with depth. Ka = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45° − φ/2), where φ is the soil friction angle.

blocks.where: P is active thrust in kN per metre length; Ka is active pressure coefficient (no unit); γ is soil unit weight in kN/m³; H is retained height in m.

blocks.text: Pressure at depth z is p = Ka γ z, so at the base p = Ka γ H. The diagram is a triangle. Thrust is its area, at H/3 above the base.
Check the wall as a rigid body under working loads before steel design.

items: Sum vertical loads: stem, base slab, soil on heel. Take moments about the toe.
Overturning: resisting moment ÷ overturning moment (P × H/3). Keep about 2.0 unless your syllabus or code says otherwise.
Sliding: μ ΣV ÷ P, about 1.5, with μ ≈ tan φ. A shear key helps if this fails.
Bearing: e = M/ΣV about base centre; pmax = (ΣV/B)(1 + 6e/B). Keep pmax below safe bearing capacity and e ≤ B/6, so no soil tension.

blocks.text: ΣV is total vertical load in kN per metre, B is base width in m, M is net moment about base centre in kN m, and e is eccentricity in m.

sections.h3: Designing the stem, heel and toe

blocks.text: Multiply earth pressure effects by 1.5. Design each part as a unit-width cantilever slab.

items: Stem: base moment 1.5 × P × H/3; base shear 1.5 × P. Main steel on soil face; nominal steel on other face.

Heel: net downward load (soil plus slab self weight minus upward soil reaction) makes it a cantilever fixed at the back face of the stem. Tension is at the top, so main steel at top of heel; nominal steel at bottom.
Toe: net upward soil pressure (minus toe self weight) makes it a cantilever fixed at the front face of the stem. Tension is at the bottom, so main steel at bottom of toe.
Check one-way shear at the stem face and anchor stem bars into the base slab for full development length.

figure.caption: For H = 4 m, γ = 18 kN/m³ and Ka = 1/3, pressure rises from zero at top to 24 kN/m² at base. Thrust is 48 kN per metre at H/3 = 1.33 m above base. The stem carries it as a cantilever into the base slab; heel and toe spread it.

spec.title: Retaining wall
spec.aria: Flow from soil pressure 24 kN per square metre to thrust 48 kN per metre at one third height, then to stem, base slab, and heel and toe.

examples.question: A wall retains 4 m of soil, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°, Ka = 1/3. Find base pressure, thrust per metre, resultant height and factored stem base moment.
steps: Base pressure p = Ka γ H = (1/3) × 18 × 4 = 24 kN/m².
Thrust P = ½ Ka γ H² = 0.5 × (1/3) × 18 × 4² = 48 kN per metre.
Resultant height = H/3 = 4/3 = 1.333 m above base.
examples.answer: Base pressure 24 kN/m²; thrust 48 kN per metre at 1.33 m above base; factored stem base moment 96 kN m per metre.
examples.check:
import math
H = 4.0
gamma = 18.0
phi = 30.0
Ka = math.tan(math.radians(45 - phi/2))**2
pa = Ka*gamma*H
P = 0.5*Ka*gamma*H**2
y = H/3
Mu = 1.5*P*y
print(round(pa,2))
print(round(P,2))
print(round(y,3))
print(round(Mu,1))

traps: Putting the resultant at H/2; a triangle's centroid is at H/3.
Writing thrust as Ka γ H and forgetting the ½.
Omitting soil on the heel from stabilizing moment; it is often largest.
Checking overturning and sliding with factored loads; stability is working-load.
Allowing e > B/6; widen base or shift stem instead.

quiz.q: What shape is the active pressure diagram for dry level backfill, and where is the resultant?
quiz.a: A triangle, zero at top and Ka γ H at base; resultant at H/3 above base.

quiz.q: Why is the resultant at H/3 rather than mid-height?
quiz.a: Pressure is largest at the bottom, so the diagram is a triangle. Its centroid is one third height from base.

quiz.q: A wall retains 5 m of soil with γ = 17 kN/m³ and Ka = 0.3. Find thrust per metre.
quiz.a: P = ½ Ka γ H² = 0.5 × 0.3 × 17 × 5² = 63.75 kN per metre.

quiz.q: For φ = 30°, find Ka and base pressure for a 3 m wall with γ = 18 kN/m³.
Average base pressure is within safe bearing capacity, but toe pressure is not. Give two remedies.
quiz.a: Widen the base slab, which lowers average and maximum pressure; or lengthen the heel by shifting the stem towards the toe, so more soil weight acts on the heel and the resultant moves back, reducing e and flattening pressure.

quiz.q: Why is stem main steel on the soil face?
quiz.a: Earth pressure bends the stem so the soil face is in tension; steel follows the tension side.

quiz.q: Why check sliding separately when overturning is satisfied?
quiz.a: Overturning is resisted by moments of vertical loads; sliding only by base friction. A wall can be safe in overturning and still slide.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, cantilever walls are often replaced by reinforced-earth, soil-nailed or anchored walls, especially above about 6 m. Finite element models check movements, not just stability. Search for reinforced earth retaining walls, soil nailing, and at-rest versus active earth pressure.
